nodes.title: Power Automate: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Power Automate. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: An IT team wants a Power Automate flow to run every weekday at 06:00 to refresh an inventory report, with no trigger from a user or another system. Which type of flow is purpose-built for this?
flashcards.back: A scheduled cloud flow runs on a recurrence (for example, every weekday at 06:00) without any external trigger, which matches the requirement exactly. Automated cloud flows are triggered by an event in a connector (a new email, a row added, etc.); instant cloud flows are triggered manually by a user from a button, mobile app or Teams; and desktop flows automate UI interactions on a Windows desktop using Power Automate for desktop (RPA) and are themselves invoked by other flows or by a user.

flashcards.front: An accounting team re-keys data every morning from a 20-year-old desktop application that has no API into a web portal. Which Power Platform capability automates this?
flashcards.back: Desktop flows are Power Automate's RPA capability: they record and replay clicks and keystrokes against applications that have no API, bridging legacy desktop software and web portals. Cloud flows need a connector or API to exist; there is no connector for the app described; virtual tables and AI Builder don't drive user interfaces.

flashcards.front: In a Power Automate cloud flow, what is the relationship between the trigger and actions?
flashcards.back: Every cloud flow begins with a single trigger — an event (automated), a button press (instant) or a schedule — and then runs one or more actions such as sending mail, updating rows or posting to Teams. Multiple triggers per flow aren't supported, and the roles aren't interchangeable: triggers start, actions execute.

flashcards.front: Expense claims over $500 must be signed off by a manager before a row is updated in Dataverse, with the decision recorded. Which Power Automate capability is designed for this?
flashcards.back: Approvals are a first-class Power Automate feature: the flow posts an actionable request (Teams, email or the Approvals center), suspends until the manager responds, records the decision and comments, then branches on the outcome. Summary emails and data alerts inform but don't gate the update; driving a mailbox with RPA to parse replies reinvents approvals badly.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
